newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Row over troops may harm Manila ties - U.S. envoy.
newsitem.headline: Row over troops may harm Manila ties - U.S. envoy.

text.p: The United States said on Thursday its security ties with the Philippines ran the risk of drifting and urged that the past be put aside so that the relationship could return to firmer ground.

U.S. Ambassador Thomas Hubbard, in a speech to businessmen, voiced concern over the inability of the two countries to resolve their dispute over who would exercise jurisdiction over U.S. soldiers accused of crimes in this former American colony.
"The longer we go without resolving this legal protections issue, the greater the risk that the security relationship will drift," he said.
The two countries have suspended joint military exercises and U.S. Navy vessels have stopped calling at Philippine ports since last year as a result of the dispute.

Hubbard said the United States was not seeking blanket immunity from Philippine law for its troops but "arrangements that clearly define those circumstances under which the Philippines or the U.S. will exercise jurisdiction if a visiting U.S. soldier is involved in a mishap or accused of a crime".
Fortunately, both countries were committed to resolving the problem and were talking to each other, he said.
"In the meantime, both sides need to re-examine in the light of a new day the baggage left over from the past," Hubbard said.
Relations between Manila and Washington cooled after the Philippine Senate rejected a new bases treaty with the United States, forcing the closure in 1992 of the last U.S. base in this country.

The jurisdiction question has long been an emotional issue for Filipinos. Nationalist groups have accused Washington of treating the Philippines as if it were still a colony after some U.S. servicemen accused of crimes were able to leave without being tried by local courts.
